w:r.w:t: Educational institutions maintain attendance records and assessment results to monitor student participation and academic progress. However, these records are often collected and reviewed through separate processes. Teachers may record attendance manually, enter examination marks in spreadsheets, and identify students requiring support only after reviewing accumulated records. This separation increases administrative effort and makes it difficult to obtain a timely, consolidated view of student performance.

Computer vision provides a means of automating attendance through face detection and recognition, while data analysis and machine learning can support the identification of academic risk. Integrating these capabilities with an academic management platform allows attendance and assessment records to support both routine administration and student guidance.

VISTA, the Visual Intelligence System for Tracking and Analysis, is developed as an integrated platform for face recognition-based attendance, academic record management, and student risk assessment. The system combines a computer vision module, a
backend, a React frontend, and an academic analysis module. Its primary user workspaces support administrators, teachers, and students.
The attendance module processes classroom photographs to detect and identify enrolled students. It uses SCRFD face detection and

, with a trained ResNet-50 classifier as a secondary identification path. Heuristic liveness checks provide an additional screening mechanism. Teachers can review recognition results and manually correct attendance when necessary.

The academic analysis component evaluates attendance patterns and assessment performance to identify students who may require support. It includes rule-based risk scoring and a separate machine learning prediction path using XG
Boost, with SHAP-based explanations. The platform also incorporates Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) analysis and an AI Study Coach that provides guidance based on recorded academic information.

VISTA brings these functions together to support attendance administration, academic monitoring, and informed intervention. Its outputs are intended to assist teachers and students while retaining human review for academic decisions.

Attendance tracking and academic performance monitoring involve recurring tasks that become difficult to manage consistently when information is distributed across registers, spreadsheets, and separate applications. Manual attendance requires classroom time and may result in incorrect entries or proxy marking. Academic records maintained independently of attendance data also make it harder to identify patterns such as declining participation accompanied by lower assessment scores.

Students face a related information gap. Knowing their current attendance percentage or examination marks does not necessarily explain how many upcoming classes they must attend to recover attendance, whether they are eligible for an improvement assessment, or what score they need in a subsequent CIE.
The problem addressed by this project is the absence of a unified platform that connects attendance capture, academic records, risk analysis, and student guidance within a consistent workflow.

Existing attendance practices include manual registers, spreadsheet-based records, RFID systems, fingerprint-based biometric devices, and face recognition applications. Each approach addresses attendance collection differently, but its usefulness depends on the operational environment.

Manual registers and spreadsheets are straightforward to use, but they require repeated teacher input and subsequent consolidation. RFID systems reduce manual entry but depend on students carrying identification cards.

Fingerprint systems verify biometric identity but generally require individual interaction with a device. Face recognition offers contactless identification, although its performance can be affected by lighting, pose, occlusion, and camera quality.
Academic management applications commonly provide facilities for storing marks and displaying attendance percentages. However, attendance capture, academic analysis, and student guidance may
remain separate functions. Teachers must then interpret the records themselves, while students receive limited assistance in understanding their recovery requirements or assessment options.
These limitations establish the need for a platform that connects attendance records with academic analysis and makes the resulting information accessible to both teachers and students.
VISTA is needed to reduce the effort involved in maintaining attendance and academic records while improving their usefulness for monitoring student progress.

Face recognition-based attendance provides an alternative to repeated manual entry. Combining automated capture with teacher review allows the system to accommodate cases where recognition is unsuccessful. Subject-wise records and manual correction facilities also help maintain a usable academic history.

Integrating attendance and assessment information supports the identification of concerns that may be less apparent when records are reviewed separately. Risk indicators and explanations can help teachers prioritize students for further review and select appropriate support measures.

The platform also addresses the student’s need for understandable academic information. CIE analysis and attendance recovery calculations translate stored records into practical guidance. The AI Study Coach provides a conversational interface to this information, supported by deterministic calculations and fallback responses.
Together, these capabilities support a more connected academic monitoring process, from attendance capture to record review and student guidance.

Attendance management and academic performance monitoring are important activities in educational institutions. Attendance records indicate student participation, while assessment results provide information about academic progress. Research in these areas includes attendance record management, facial recognition, classroom engagement analysis, and prediction of student academic performance [1], [21], [22], [24].

Automated attendance systems use facial recognition to associate captured student images with registered identities. Their practical operation involves image acquisition, face detection, identity comparison, and attendance recording. The effectiveness of the complete process depends on capture conditions,
quality, recognition decisions, and the correctness of the resulting records [6], [24].

Academic monitoring extends beyond identifying whether a student is present. Previous academic information can support performance prediction, while attendance records can contribute to reviewing participation and eligibility [1], [21]. Other research combines attendance with emotion analysis to investigate classroom engagement [22].

This chapter reviews selected studies from the supplied bibliography, compares their contributions, and identifies the requirements motivating VISTA. The discussion distinguishes attendance recognition, administrative record management, engagement analysis, and academic prediction because these tasks require different forms of evaluation.

The study demonstrates the application of machine learning to educational records rather than limiting academic monitoring to the storage and display of marks [1].

The work is relevant to VISTA’s academic analysis component because it establishes a connection between historical records and predictive modelling. However, the usefulness of a predictive model depends on the information available, the definition of its target outcome, and the population represented in its data.

For VISTA, this study motivates examining attendance and assessment information together while documenting the limitations of the experimental academic risk classifier. Results from a different dataset cannot independently establish the reliability of VISTA’s predictions.
2.2.2 Machine Learning Based Face Recognition Attendance

“Smart Face Recognition Based Attendance System Using ML Algorithm” (2022) examines the application of machine learning to face-based attendance recording. It represents the use of automated identity processing as part of an attendance-management application [4].

Its relevance to VISTA is the connection between recognition and the administrative task of marking attendance. The recognition stage must produce an identity that can be associated with an enrolled student before the system records a confirmed attendance outcome.

The study’s title and publication record establish its subject area. No numerical performance comparison is made here because comparable experimental conditions and results have not been established for this review.
2.2.3 Face Recognition Automatic Class Attendance System

“Face Recognition Automatic Class Attendance System (FRACAS)” (2019) investigates facial recognition for acquiring classroom attendance. The work addresses the time and authentication concerns involved in attendance collection and considers ordinary changes in facial appearance [6].

FRACAS provides an earlier example of connecting biometric identity recognition with classroom administration. Its relevance lies in treating attendance as an application workflow that requires both identification and record creation.
For VISTA, this motivates the association of recognition results with registered student records and the availability of teacher review when the automated result requires correction.
“Student Attendance Control System with Face Recognition Based on Neural Network” (2021) investigates neural-network-based facial recognition within an attendance-control system [9].

The study is relevant to the use of learned facial representations for identifying students. It also places recognition within a record-management application, where identification outcomes must be converted into usable attendance information.

For VISTA, this work provides background for considering recognition as one component of a larger system. The presence of a neural network does not independently establish accurate attendance recording; the complete workflow still requires evaluation.
2.2.5 Face Recognition Attendance for Online Classes
“Face Recognition Attendance System for Online Classes” (2022) examines attendance identification in an online teaching context [13].

The study is relevant because attendance capture can occur in different environments. Images obtained during online classes differ from classroom photographs in their layout, camera positioning, image quality, and visibility of participants.

VISTA focuses on processing classroom images and maintaining academic records. Consequently, results from online-class attendance cannot be treated as directly equivalent to results obtained from classroom group photographs.
2.2.6 Automated Attendance Using Facial Recognition and Python

“Automated Attendance Monitoring System using Real-Time Facial Recognition and Python based Computer Vision Techniques” (2025) addresses attendance automation through facial recognition and computer vision [14].

The work contributes to the application background for implementing attendance processing using a software-based vision pipeline. Its relevance to VISTA is the practical connection between image processing and attendance administration.

The title identifies the implementation focus, but it does not establish an accuracy or processing-time result for VISTA. The present project therefore reports its own available recognition and timing evidence separately.
2.2.7 Smart Attendance Using Local Binary Pattern Histograms

Sharma et al. (2024), in “Smart Attendance System Using Face Recognition,” describe an attendance application using the Local Binary Pattern Histogram algorithm. Their workflow maintains facial profiles, performs recognition during attendance sessions, updates attendance information in an Excel sheet, and communicates compiled records to faculty through email [16].

This work illustrates the importance of connecting recognition with an output that teachers can use. Attendance automation includes maintaining and communicating records, rather than stopping at the display of a recognized identity.

VISTA follows a database-backed approach and presents information through role-based interfaces. This difference concerns the organisation of the application and does not establish that one system achieves higher recognition accuracy than the other.
“Attendance Management System Using Facial Recognition” (2022) addresses the use of face recognition within an attendance-management application [17].

The study contributes to the broader application context in which biometric recognition supports an administrative process. For VISTA, the corresponding implementation requirements include student identification, attendance creation, record retrieval, and correction of unsuccessful or incorrect outcomes.
No numerical comparison is presented because consistent datasets, hardware, and evaluation procedures have not been established across the reviewed applications.

Acharya’s attendance-management preprint (2024) describes software for maintaining daily attendance information and retrieving attendance records for students and classes. It also discusses the use of attendance information when reviewing attendance eligibility [21].
The work provides an administrative perspective that complements face-recognition studies. Automated image processing is useful only when its outputs become consistent, accessible records.

For VISTA, this motivates subject-wise attendance storage, retrieval of student histories, and calculations that explain attendance status. It also supports retaining manual entry as part of the academic workflow.

(2026), in “Integrating Attendance Tracking and Emotion Detection for Enhanced Student Engagement in Smart Classrooms,” present SCASED, an IoT-based system combining attendance tracking with facial emotion analysis. The system uses a Raspberry Pi camera, OpenCV, and a fine-tuned MobileNetV2 model [22].

Its session-based workflow records attendance once per session and then continues monitoring selected learning-related emotional states. The authors report 89.5% emotion-classification accuracy using the DAiSEE dataset. This value concerns emotion classification and is not an attendance-recognition accuracy result [22].

The study demonstrates one way of extending attendance with classroom analytics. VISTA has a different analytical scope: it uses recorded attendance and assessment information for academic monitoring rather than inferring emotional states from student faces.

Pires et al. (2025), in “End-to-end automated student attendance recording system using surveillance camera,” investigate attendance recording using classroom surveillance images. Their evaluation includes five classroom sessions from a public dataset and three sessions collected in a school [24].

The study compares recognition alternatives under different image-quality and student-positioning conditions. ResNet29 performed best among the evaluated alternatives for the reported attendance-marking task [24].

This work is particularly relevant to VISTA because it examines the relationship between classroom capture conditions and the resulting attendance records. It motivates evaluating complete attendance outcomes rather than treating isolated identity classification as sufficient evidence of application reliability.

The reviewed literature establishes existing approaches to face-based attendance, administrative record management, classroom engagement analysis, and academic prediction. The practical integration requirement addressed by VISTA is to connect selected functions within a common academic workflow.

VISTA combines classroom image processing with teacher review, subject-wise attendance records, assessment information, CIE calculations, academic risk indicators, and student guidance. Its purpose is to make these records available to the users responsible for maintaining and acting on them.

The project also distinguishes between operational rules and experimental prediction. Rule-based risk indicators and trained-model outputs are maintained as separate analytical paths. This prevents their results from being presented as one uniformly validated prediction mechanism.

Another requirement concerns the usefulness of academic information to students. Attendance percentages and assessment marks describe the current position but do not necessarily explain the next action. VISTA addresses this through attendance recovery calculations, absence allowances, improvement eligibility checks, and required-score estimates.
These requirements define the scope of the proposed integration. They do not imply that every reviewed system lacks these functions or that similar combinations are absent from all previous research.
The proposed work is motivated by the effort involved in collecting attendance, maintaining assessment records, reviewing academic progress, and explaining improvement requirements.

Face-based processing provides an alternative attendance-capture method. Teacher review and manual entry support cases where image quality or recognition outcomes require intervention. Maintaining the resulting information within a shared database allows attendance and assessment records to support further academic review.

The project also addresses the need to translate recorded values into practical guidance. A student may know the current attendance percentage without knowing how many consecutive classes are required to reach a target. Similarly, assessment marks become more useful when accompanied by CIE eligibility and required-score calculations.

VISTA therefore brings attendance processing, academic records, analysis, and guidance together through administrator, teacher, and student interfaces. The intended outcome is a more connected academic monitoring process with human oversight.

Face size, lighting, camera angle, pose, and occlusion can influence recognition outcomes. Classroom evaluation therefore requires representative images rather than relying entirely on prepared facial samples [24].
A detected face must be associated with an enrolled student before a confirmed attendance entry is created. Incorrect matches and unsuccessful recognition require review mechanisms.

The meaning of an attendance session must remain consistent across capture, storage, correction, and percentage calculation. Inconsistent counting can affect attendance summaries even when identity recognition is correct.

Predictive analysis depends on the completeness and meaning of its inputs. Missing assessment results, inconsistent attendance records, and differences between student populations can reduce the usefulness of academic predictions.

Recognition, database operations, academic calculations, and user interfaces must exchange consistent information. A functioning component does not independently establish a functioning complete workflow.

Facial images, identity-linked representations, and academic records require controlled handling. Students also need a process for challenging incorrect records. Academic risk indicators require interpretation by teachers before decisions affecting students are made.

The reviewed studies use different datasets, operating environments, recognition methods, and output definitions. Their results therefore cannot support a universal accuracy claim for automated attendance or academic prediction.

Publication titles and implementation descriptions also provide different levels of evidence from documented experiments. Where comparable experimental results are unavailable, this chapter limits its comparison to the stated application scope.

Attendance automation, emotion monitoring, and academic prediction require separate interpretation. A successful result in one task does not establish reliability in another. Likewise, an attendance screenshot or academic dashboard does not independently demonstrate recognition accuracy or predictive validity.
These limitations motivate a component-wise evaluation of VISTA, with clear distinctions between measured results, calculated estimates, demonstration records, and expected policy outcomes.

This chapter presents the architecture and methodology of VISTA, the Visual Intelligence System for Tracking and Analysis. The system integrates face recognition-based attendance, academic record management, risk assessment, CIE evaluation, and student guidance through a common web platform.

The architecture describes the responsibilities of the system components and their communication. The methodology explains how classroom images and academic records are processed to produce attendance results, risk indicators, assessment summaries, and guidance.

VISTA follows a modular design comprising a presentation layer, an application layer, an intelligence layer, and a data layer. This organization allows the recognition, academic analysis, and user interface components to be developed and evaluated separately while supporting integrated workflows.
The system architecture connects browser-based user interfaces with backend services, recognition models, academic analysis functions, and persistent records.
The presentation layer is implemented using React and Vite. It provides three primary workspaces:
Supports management of users, students, classes, subjects, teacher assignments, and academic records.
Supports classroom image capture, attendance review, manual corrections, assessment entry, and student record viewing.
Provides personal attendance and assessment information, subject details, notifications, and access to the Study Coach.

Testing and evaluation examine whether VISTA performs its intended functions and establish the limits of the available evidence. The system combines recognition models, academic calculations, database operations, and user interfaces, so each component requires a suitable verification approach.
This chapter presents the testing strategy, functional test coverage, face recognition results, academic risk-model evaluation, and processing-time observations.

The numerical results are taken from the recorded project evaluations. They represent previously recorded experiments rather than a fresh execution of the complete application. Functional test definitions are distinguished from confirmed execution outcomes, and calculated scaling estimates are identified separately from measured timings.
The testing strategy is divided into component testing, integration testing, and application workflow testing.
Component testing examines individual functions independently of the complete application.
The vision tests address embedding operations, cosine similarity, matching, gallery preference, liveness checks, and model loading.

Academic analysis tests address risk categories, override conditions, incomplete information, and zero-session handling. Additional tests cover CIE eligibility, absent assessments, best-two-score selection, and required-score calculations.
Integration testing examines communication between backend operations, database records, and analytical functions.
Examples include authentication, attendance submission, student record retrieval, risk recalculation, notifications, and report export.

Some attendance integration tests replace recognition with controlled responses. These tests verify backend handling of recognition results; they do not measure the accuracy of the actual recognition models.
Workflow testing examines complete user tasks, including:
Classroom image capture and attendance review.
Student access to personal academic information.
Study Coach guidance and conversation management.

VISTA supports classroom attendance recording by identifying registered students from classroom images. Face-based processing can reduce the effort involved in individual roll calls, particularly when several students are visible in the same image. Teachers can review recognition results and use manual attendance entry when image quality, occlusion, or recognition confidence requires intervention.

The platform combines attendance and assessment information to provide a consolidated view of student progress. Teachers can review attendance shortages, low marks, and changes in performance, while students can access their own academic summaries. This information can support discussions about academic improvement.

The rule-based risk mechanism identifies patterns such as low attendance, declining marks, and consecutive absences. These indicators can help teachers identify students who may benefit from counselling, additional learning support, or attendance recovery plans. Intervention decisions remain subject to teacher judgement and the accuracy of the underlying records.

The separate trained-model pipeline provides an experimental basis for further research into academic risk classification. Its current evaluation does not establish sufficient reliability for independent institutional decision-making.

The CIE module supports assessment calculations, improvement eligibility checks, and required-score estimates. It distinguishes between pending assessments, recorded absences, and available scores. When a third assessment is attempted, the applicable best-two-score calculation supports consistent result preparation.
Students can use these calculations to understand their current assessment position, while teachers can use them when reviewing improvement eligibility and final results.

The Study Coach provides guidance using the authenticated student’s recorded academic information. It supports practical queries concerning attendance recovery, allowable future absences, and assessment targets.

Deterministic calculations provide the numerical basis for this guidance. Optional language-model services can present the information conversationally, while a fallback mechanism provides responses when those services are unavailable.

Role-based interfaces organise access for administrators, teachers, and students. Administrators can manage institutional records, teachers can maintain academic information, and students can review their own progress. Bringing these activities together can reduce the effort involved in consulting separate attendance and assessment records.

8.3.3 Interpretable Risk Indicators and Experimental Classification

VISTA includes a rule-based scoring mechanism with defined components and a separate machine-learning pipeline. This separation supports transparent reporting of operational rules and experimental model results.

The CIE module supports eligibility checks, required-score calculations, and final-result computation. It treats pending assessments and absences as distinct states rather than automatically interpreting them as zero scores.

The Study Coach connects guidance to the authenticated student’s recorded information. Attendance and assessment calculations support concrete recommendations that students can use when planning improvement.
Administrator, teacher, and student interfaces organise access according to user responsibilities. This supports academic administration while allowing students to review their own information.

The recorded classifier evaluation covers a restricted set of identities. It does not establish recognition performance across different classrooms, cameras, lighting conditions, seating arrangements, and student populations.

Recognition outcomes depend on the selected similarity threshold. A stricter threshold can reduce incorrect identification while rejecting more valid students. The appropriate operating threshold therefore requires validation under representative conditions.

Heuristic liveness checks do not establish robust resistance to printed photographs, screen replays, or other presentation attacks. Stronger protection requires dedicated implementation and evaluation.

Attendance summaries, CIE calculations, risk indicators, and student guidance depend on complete and accurate source records. Missing assessments, inconsistent session definitions, and outdated information can affect the usefulness of the results.
The processing-time projections for increasing face counts are estimates. They do not establish measured performance during live classroom attendance processing.
Deployment configurations provide a starting point for operation, but sustained availability, concurrent usage, recovery procedures, and optional service integrations require further testing.

Future evaluation should include more students, varied seating positions, different camera angles, changing illumination, and partial occlusion. Testing across multiple classrooms would provide stronger evidence of practical recognition performance.
Evaluation should report incorrect identification and rejection alongside overall accuracy. Threshold selection should use separate validation data, followed by assessment on an independent test set.

The recognition pipeline can be extended with a validated presentation-attack detection method. Testing should include printed photographs and screen-based replay attempts to assess the effectiveness of the protection.

The trained risk model should be developed using appropriately authorised and anonymised institutional data. Future work should investigate class imbalance, feature quality, risk-category definitions, and the causes of poor LOW-risk detection.

Comparisons should include simple baseline models and report per-class precision, recall, and F1-score. Evaluation across different semesters or student cohorts would help determine whether the model generalises beyond its training data.

Future versions can allow teachers to record counselling, attendance recovery plans, and academic support measures. Tracking subsequent student progress would help assess whether the information provided by VISTA contributes to useful interventions.

The Study Coach can be extended with approved course resources and more detailed study planning. Its responses should be evaluated for factual consistency, appropriate use of student records, and agreement with deterministic calculations.
Clear handling of incomplete records and unavailable model services should remain part of this development.

Integration with learning management systems and institutional academic systems could reduce duplicate data entry. This would require consistent identifiers for students, subjects, assessments, and attendance sessions, together with validation of imported records.

Future testing should measure the complete attendance workflow, including image upload, detection, recognition, database operations, and result delivery. Concurrent-user tests and extended deployment trials would help establish realistic capacity and resource requirements.
Backup restoration, service recovery, and monitoring should also be verified before sustained institutional use.

Further development should strengthen biometric data retention and deletion controls, access auditing, and secure storage. Students should also have a clear process for reporting incorrect attendance or assessment records.
Responsive interfaces, keyboard navigation, accessible visual design, and clearer error messages would improve usability across devices and user groups.

VISTA connects attendance management, academic monitoring, and student guidance through shared records and role-based access. The project provides a foundation for further development, while its evaluation identifies the areas requiring improvement. Representative testing, accurate academic data, teacher oversight, and reliable deployment will be central to its practical adoption in educational institutions.
